summary: Extends the Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT) based on the SHAKEN specification from ATIS and the SIP Forum. It adds levels of confidence in the originating identity and a way to identify the origin of a call. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A signed note attached to a phone call that says how sure the carrier is about who is calling, to fight fake caller IDs.

questions: what is the attest claim in passport
what are attestation levels a b c
subtitle: Two extra claims that let a phone carrier say how sure it is about a caller and where the call began.

tldr.problem: Telephone calls today come from both VoIP and older TDM/SS7 networks, so a signed caller identity needs to say how well the provider actually knows the caller, and where in its network the call started.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a PASSporT extension named shaken with two claims: attest, with levels A, B or C, and origid, a UUID that identifies the call's origin point.
tldr.outcome: Receivers get signed information about attestation level and call origin, supporting traceback of illegitimate calls. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8588 is a Proposed Standard from May 2019, and the metadata lists no document obsoleting or updating it. IANA registered the attest and origid claims and the shaken PASSporT type.

sections.title: SHAKEN and PASSporT
sections.content:
The SHAKEN framework from ATIS and the SIP Forum uses the STIR protocols to cryptographically validate the authorized originator of a call made with SIP. It builds on PASSporT (RFC 8225), SIP Authenticated Identity Management (RFC 8224) and the STIR certificate framework (RFC 8226).

Today's telephone network carries traffic from both VoIP and TDM/SS7, so a PASSporT signature may represent direct or indirect call origination. This document specifies SHAKEN's attestation levels and origination identifier as claims that extend the base PASSporT claims.

A PASSporT is a JSON Web Token (RFC 7519) made for securing the identity of the initiator of personal communication.
sections.eli5: Phone calls come from old and new kinds of networks. This note adds two extra facts to the signed caller ID so everyone knows how far to trust it.

sections.title: The shaken Extension
sections.content:
The extension adds two claims for a service provider to signal more than the telephone identity. The first, attest, helps bridge the move from today's network, which has calls with no authentication and non-SIP signaling that cannot use PASSporT.

The second is a unique origination identifier the provider should use to identify different sources of calls, supporting a traceback mechanism for enforcement and for finding the source of illegitimate calls.

The compact form of PASSporT is not specified here and is not specified for use in SHAKEN.
sections.eli5: The first fact tells how sure the carrier is. The second helps investigators follow a bad call back to where it started.

sections.title: The attest and origid Claims
sections.content:
The attest claim identifies the provider vouching for the call and what it is attesting to. Its value is one of three letters: A for Full Attestation, B for Partial Attestation and C for Gateway Attestation. The levels are defined in the SHAKEN specification.

In outline, full means the provider can fully attest to the calling identity. Partial means the provider originated the call but cannot fully attest to the identity. Gateway, the lowest level, means the provider received the call from a telephone gateway that does not support PASSporT or STI.

The origid claim is a Universally Unique Identifier (UUID) as defined in RFC 4122.
sections.eli5: A means the carrier is very sure, B means it knows the call started with it but not who exactly, and C means it only passed the call along from an old phone link.

sections.title: Example PASSporT and Use in SIP
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example with protected header fields alg of ES256, typ of passport, ppt of shaken and an x5u certificate URL. The payload carries attest, dest, iat, orig and origid.

Use in SIP is formally defined in the SHAKEN specification, using the SIP Identity header field from RFC 8224. The claim keys MUST appear in lexicographic order, following Section 9 of RFC 8225, so the payload order is attest, dest, iat, orig, origid.
sections.eli5: The signed note has to list its facts in alphabetical order, like names on a class roll, so every computer reads it the same way.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Security of the PASSporT object itself is as described in RFC 8225. RFC 8224 compares the dest, orig and iat claims against the SIP message. The new attest and origid claims are not part of that check. They carry extra information from signer to consumer, with the same integrity protection and non-repudiation as the base claims.

On privacy, origid is meant to be opaque, to limit what it reveals about where a call originated. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to generate a unique value per call so only the generator can tell whether two values name the same element. A shared or related origid could let recipients correlate calls and learn, for instance, that callers use a common gateway. SHAKEN PASSporTs are expected to be shared only within an RFC 3324 trust domain and stripped on exit.
sections.eli5: The secret origin code should be different every time. If it were always the same, someone could notice the pattern and learn things about the caller.

items.label: Full Attestation
items.desc: The provider can fully attest to the calling identity.

items.label: Partial Attestation
items.desc: The provider originated the call but cannot fully attest to the identity.

items.label: Gateway Attestation
items.desc: The lowest level: the call came from a gateway that does not support PASSporT or STI.
